status: All eight halls reviewed in this pass; embodied development continues
summary: The closing sequence moves from distinctions, participation and disagreement to shared objects, connections and possible bodies. The final assembly follows a reusable instance through changing form; the ledger returns us to the opening clock and to a particular thing we want to make. This closes the review pass, while full-scale inhabitable encounters remain a priority.

items.title: Do the branches actually meet?
items.description: JUNCTION leaves a gap. OVERLAP rotates both branches inward while their feet retain their positions. The visitor can remove the glowing marker to inspect what is there. The artifact moves nearer arrival; every supporting family stays.

items.after:

items.after:

items.title: A revision is not a settlement
items.description: The earlier proposed experiment is now available. DISPUTE marks an existing piece; REVISE changes its pose while preserving its source. The dispute stays. The counter distinguishes changing a piece from adding one.
captions: Piece 31, source P5: disputed, no revisions.
Same piece: one visitor revision; forty pieces and forty additions remain.
items.image_note: Same camera and selected piece. The visible shape change is modest; the frame and readout identify it. This is geometric revision without semantic validation.
items.text_kind: book — from arrival to reconsideration
items.before: For a proposed extension, mark one contribution as disputed and keep its source visible. Let revision change an existing piece instead of always adding another. The comparison would show how maintaining knowledge differs from celebrating uninterrupted growth.
items.after:
Choose a piece and press DISPUTE. Its frame turns red. Press REVISE and watch that same piece turn and change height. The pile has not gained a piece; the revision count has increased. The source is still named, and the change is attributed to VISITOR. The red frame stays. A change has happened, but who agreed that the dispute was settled?

Here revision is a geometric operation we have supplied. It has no evidence to weigh and no argument to answer. The original and previous poses remain in the record, but there is no complete history you can browse. Keeping a name and a trace makes reconsideration possible; it does not perform the reconsideration for us.

items.title: What survives the next version?
items.description: The historic CONTRIBUTORS discrepancy remains part of the chapter. PARTICIPATIONS names repeated source-version attendance; EVER counts distinct nodes across versions. A previous version is retained in memory, without a full history browser.
captions: Side view of the revised piece: its source and visitor intervention remain named.
Version 2: three arrivals, two current sources, six ever-seen sources and eight participations.
items.image_note: 39 runtime checks, seven selected walking segments and 79 content checks pass. These images differ in camera and version. Two supporting scene files exist but their museum lookup still rejects them; their restoration is recorded separately. Headset testing remains open.
items.text_kind: book — from arrival to reconsideration
items.before: Every accepted facet increments the edit count. The Boolean array _seen_peers lets the same source count only once within a version. On the next version those flags clear while the totals persist. A number labelled CONTRIBUTORS can therefore outgrow the twelve source positions. The code tells us what was counted more precisely than the label does.
items.after:
Every accepted facet increments the addition count. The Boolean array _seen_peers lets the same source count only once within a version. On the next version those flags clear while the totals persist. In the earlier display, a number labelled CONTRIBUTORS could therefore outgrow the twelve source positions. That number is now called PARTICIPATIONS. SOURCES counts distinct nodes in this version; EVER counts distinct nodes across versions. The old discrepancy was useful: it showed how a label could quietly turn repeated attendance into an expanding community.

Before pressing VERSION, look once more at the disputed piece. The next form starts empty. Its current source count begins again while additions and participations carry on; EVER does not count an old source as a new one. The device keeps only the previous version in memory. What would have to survive for someone else to understand why you changed that piece?

items.title: The points stay; the relations change
items.description: LINKS compares one and three earlier neighbours without drawing another set of points. NODE names the selected arrival and counts its degree. The manuscript keeps no named root separate from equal influence.
captions: One link: 24 points, 22 edges, two connected components. Node 3 has degree 3.
Three links: the same 24 points, 65 edges, one component. Node 3 has degree 8.
items.image_note: Actual revised museum states from the same camera and sample sequence. Positions are identical; only the connection rule changes. The surrounding circular frame is not a graph edge.
items.text_kind: book — follow the relation, then test its loss
items.before: The rule still has consequences worth inspecting. Earlier nodes are available to be chosen for longer, and spatially well-placed nodes can attract many nearby additions. A network without a designated root can develop busy regions and uneven degrees. “No root” describes part of the construction; it does not prove that every participant has equal influence.
items.after:
The rule still has consequences worth inspecting. Earlier nodes are available to be chosen for longer, and spatially well-placed nodes can attract many nearby additions. A network without a designated root can develop busy regions and uneven degrees. “No root” describes part of the construction; it does not prove that every participant has equal influence.

Hold an arrangement and press LINKS. The points stay where they are while the rule changes between one and three earlier neighbours. What disappears without any point moving? With one link per new node, the two starting points remain in separate trees. Three links allow routes between those trees. A rule that never names a root can still grow ancestors.

items.title: What survives the same loss?
items.description: The previously proposed removal is now a visitor operation. CUT removes a node and its incident links, leaving a small grey ghost. No new connections are created to replace them.
captions: Node 3 removed from the one-link graph: four components and 19 surviving edges.
The same node removed under three links: one component and 57 surviving edges.
items.image_note: Same camera, points and removed node. The denser version survives this removal; the comparison does not claim that any graph withstands any cut.
items.text_kind: book — follow the relation, then test its loss
items.before: Find a node with several visible links. Imagine removing it and predict whether the remaining pieces would still connect. Graph theory gave us the tools to ask this precisely. The present exhibit does not offer deletion, so treat the prediction as a proposed test rather than evidence that every rhizome repairs itself.
items.after:
Find a node with several visible links. Before pressing CUT, predict whether the remaining pieces will still connect. The node becomes a small grey ghost and its links disappear. COMPONENTS counts the separate connected groups, including a point left alone. Follow the remaining paths before trusting the number. A crossing of lines is not a junction unless they meet at a node.

Press CUT again to restore it, then change LINKS and remove the same node. Does the loss divide this version too? Nothing repairs itself while you watch; the machine holds the graph so you can inspect what survived. Restoration puts back the missing point and its old links. These are different acts: surviving a loss, repairing a relation, undoing a removal. The display lets us compare the first and perform the last. Repair still needs a rule.

items.title: What was decided before growth began?

items.text_kind: book — follow the relation, then test its loss

Press GROW to hold the arrivals. REPLAY returns to the first two points; STEP admits one more and waits. You can follow the next addition without losing it in the next ten.

The exhibit starts with two unconnected nodes. Each new shoot is placed within a fixed ring-shaped region and linked to up to three of the nearest existing nodes. Repeating this rule builds a graph from local proximity. At forty nodes, the display holds. REPLAY uses the same sequence of positions, so another attempt can meet the same arrangement.

The ring does not spread with the shoots. The machine keeps finding new places inside a boundary it chose before the network began. Something is growing, but its territory has already been given.

items.title: One instance, another body
items.description: An amber ring follows the same carrier from body joint to chair panel. Unused carriers move visibly to the sides, leaving room to see the assembly. The collection is mutable; its catalogue, target positions and declared bonds shape what it can become.
captions: A body assembled from the catalogue. The ring follows its central joint.
The same instance becomes a chair panel; surplus body parts join the surrounding inventory.
items.image_note: Current Godot states, same camera and persistent instance. Eighteen simulated seconds of the actual spring calculation settle each form. These are visual parts, not a body you can wear or a chair that supports you.
items.text_kind: book
items.before: Choose a recognisable piece in the floating inventory and keep it in view as an assembly begins. Watch it approach a position and acquire relations to other pieces. Stay through another floating phase and a later assembly. Notice whether the same part instance keeps its shape and colour when it takes a new role.
items.after:
Walk around the floating inventory. Find the piece carrying an amber ring and keep it in view as an assembly begins. Watch it approach a position and acquire relations to other pieces. Stay through another floating phase and a later assembly. The ring stays with one instance. Does the shape inside it stay the same?

The floating inventory is not a fixed stock of materials. The assembly can turn the same carrier from a sphere into a panel; if it needs more carriers, the program can make them. The amber ring lets you follow that permission. What stays the same is the instance, while its shape, name and place in the body can change. The catalogue limits the available descriptions, but an initial shortage of panels does not prevent a chair.

Can local connections build a network without first choosing its centre?

Watch for a new node and follow the segments it adds. Compare a crowded part of the structure with a sparse part. Predict which existing nodes are likely to receive the next connections, then check the new shoot against your prediction.
items.after:
From outside, you can follow several passages with your eyes. One rises across another. Openings disappear into the tangle. There seems to be a way through.

Inside, the wall takes away that view. The passage divides. A coloured light gathers at a junction; further on, another opening offers another direction. You can leave a place and find it again without walking back along the way you came.

Try returning to the violet light by a different passage. What did you recognise first: the colour, the opening, the direction from which you expected it? A place can become familiar before you can draw its position in the whole.

How can one collection of parts become several recognisable structures?

<!-- @MolecularDesigner -->

Walk around the floating inventory. Find the piece carrying an amber ring and keep it in view as an assembly begins. Watch it approach a position and acquire relations to other pieces. Stay through another floating phase and a later assembly. The ring stays with one instance. Does the shape inside it stay the same?

The scene gives the parts eight seconds to float and eighteen to approach an assembly. At this scale a body stands beside yours; a chair is something you can circle. The catalogue also includes insects, trees and other structures. Bond lines update between the assigned parts as they move towards their targets. Unused pieces drift to the sides, leaving the changing body in the middle.
items.after:
A hand waits at the end of an arm. Take it a little farther than an arm ought to reach. The elbow stays behind. The slender connection follows, becoming longer. Let go.

The body keeps your alteration.

It stands close to your height, with warm metal joints and just enough between them for you to recognise shoulders, knees, a head. You may already have begun correcting it. Bringing the hand back. Making the two sides agree. Nobody in the room asked for symmetry; perhaps you brought that instruction with you.

Try leaving the hand somewhere else. Move around the body. From one side it is reaching; from another, falling. Lower its head towards the hand. A few displacements make a gesture, and the gesture makes you read the whole arrangement again. The little spheres have no expression. Where did the expression enter?

items.description: A changed release in Assembly keeps a local pose. The final hall reconstructs it beside its starting arrangement; the ledger reads that same record. The chapter investigates what survived and what was never retained.

After four controlled joint changes in Assembly: the final hall reconstructs the saved pose beside its starting arrangement.

items.before:
Can you name one person a useful design choice could leave out?

<!-- @accountability_ledger -->

Read one complete pair on the ledger before it scrolls away. Choose a concrete case, such as a short name field and someone whose name exceeds it. Say what the designer probably gained, what the person encounters, and one change that could reduce the difficulty.

The exhibit cycles through prewritten examples of choices and exclusions. A new example arrives every six seconds; six lines remain visible at once, and an amber mark accompanies a new entry. Its form resembles an accumulating record, but these entries are examples: it is not recording your visit, saving your discussion or certifying that any problem has been repaired.
items.after:
Look for the hand you moved.

It has crossed the threshold without making the journey. Beyond the ledger, an amber body holds the last pose kept in the Assembly Laboratory. The blue body beside it holds the starting arrangement. Walk between them. The elbow, the lowered head, the hand left too far away: a difference you made in another room can now be met from another side.

If you came straight here, the amber space will be empty. There is a place for a record, but no pose has yet been kept. That emptiness belongs to the work too.

The two bodies need not be dramatically different. Perhaps you moved one hand and decided that was enough. Perhaps you made the figure almost unrecognisable. Each still has thirteen joints and twelve connections. The totals agree. The bodies may no longer seem to.

items.title: Assembly: a body with weight
items.description: The familiar body becomes a grabbable physics puppet. Pulling a hand carries the elbow and shoulder; release lets it fall. Compare it with the gold body that keeps a pose.
captions: The body hangs at standing scale. Coral rings mark the parts you can take.
A controlled hand pull travels through the elbow and shoulder. A thin elastic tether makes the distance from the held target visible.
The hand has been released. Gravity, rotating joints and floor contact settle the body.
